 Jayden Daniels and the new-look Commanders offense haven't yet completely launched. Patrick Smith / Getty Images 
 By Nicki Jhabvala Nov. 5, 2026 Updated Nov. 12, 2026 5:10 pm EST Share article 28 The Athletic has live coverage of Commanders vs. Giants on “Thursday Night Football.” 
 The Washington Commanders didn’t start over completely after their 2025 season ended with only a handful of wins. A month after the team moved on from its previous coordinators, coach Dan Quinn reintroduced David Blough, previously the assistant quarterbacks coach, as his new play caller and they laid out their basic vision of the offense.
 Advertisement
 Blough’s would be “an aggressive, balanced attack,” Quinn said, with more under-center formations and a departure from the no-huddle system Jayden Daniels had grown accustomed to over the past two years. It would require the young quarterback to get comfortable with relaying play calls — some of them lengthy — then quickly reading the defense to make any checks at the line of scrimmage.
 Among the more noticeable changes: Daniels would work under center more and no longer operate almost exclusively from the shotgun formation.
 “I think it opens up some different schemes in the run game, some things that I believe in,” Blough explained in February. “It opens up different play actions and keepers and getting him on the perimeter in different ways. I think there’s a level of communication that happens under center. … I think a lot of teams that you saw even playing deep into the playoffs, it was something that was a foundation of what they did.”
 The goal, both Quinn and Blough said, was to create a more explosive system that would take advantage of Daniels’ accuracy and running without asking him to do everything for the offense.
 Throughout the offseason, Blough, a first-time play caller, collaborated with his assistants and sought the input of his players as they built a system they said would be exclusively theirs. The foundation was an amalgamation of the offenses Blough ran during his years as a quarterback, and drawing from the offenses run by Washington’s previous play caller, Kliff Kingsbury, as well as Vikings head coach Kevin O’Connell and even Louisville coach Jeff Brohm, whom Blough played for at Purdue.
 The crux of the Commanders’ offense, however, would draw from Ben Johnson, Blough’s former coordinator in Detroit who has since transformed the Chicago Bears’ offense with his heavy use of play action, multiple tight end sets, outside zone run concepts and pre-snap motion.
 Advertisement
 “We’re gonna make the same things look different and different things look the same and teach in a creative way,” Blough said. “And there’s things that I think will be really evident when they come to life on the field.”
 At times, that has been the case, like when Blough dialed up the same formation in the red zone in Week 8 against the Eagles as he had in Week 1. Both plays resulted in touchdown passes to Stefon Diggs. On the first, Diggs ran a quick seam route out of a bunch set to score on a 10-yard pass . Then on Sunday, Diggs faked that same seam route before cutting outside to run a fade for an 8-yard touchdown .
 But Washington’s grand plan for transforming its offense has yet to fully take shape. A slew of injuries to key players hindered the transition, but the group’s bigger issues have often been self-inflicted, with pre-snap penalties, clock-management gaffes, poor protection, a lagging run game and many missed opportunities.
 More significant: Daniels has yet to display the same comfort in Blough’s system that he seemed to instantly find in Kingsbury’s offense, which was intentionally built around some of the same concepts and formations Daniels was accustomed to in college.
 That contrast will be at the forefront this weekend when the Commanders host a depleted Los Angeles Rams team that now includes Kingsbury as its assistant head coach, and Brian Johnson, Washington’s former assistant head coach and pass game coordinator, as a senior offensive assistant.
 While Blough has shown flashes of potentially being a great play caller, Commanders coaches and players have admitted they’re not fully adjusted to the new offense. The numbers also indicate the system, as initially advertised, isn’t fully formed.
 Have we jumped the shark with all the 'checkdown merchant' talk in the NFL? Robert Mays and Derrik Klassen 
 The two hallmarks of Blough’s changes are evident: While the Commanders still rank among the top three teams in shotgun percentage, they’ve increased their use of under-center formations to 28.1 percent of dropbacks, up from an average of 10.9 percent over the previous two seasons. And their use of no-huddle has plummeted to only 8.2 percent this season, down from their league-high 61.2 percent from 2024 to ‘25, according to TruMedia.
 Advertisement
 But the system hasn’t consistently produced the results Quinn and Blough had hoped. According to NextGen Stats, Washington’s EPA per play from under center is minus-0.24, the lowest in the league through Week 8, and its play-action rate (15.8 percent) and explosive play rate (10.5 percent) are both down from the previous two seasons.
 Some expected key features have not yet come to pass, in part because of injuries. The running backs room has had a revolving door, with Jacory Croskey-Merritt and Jeremy McNichols now both on injured reserve, thus putting more on Daniels. The Commanders’ non-QB rush EPA per game is minus-2.94, 22nd in the NFL, per TruMedia.
 The Commanders also lacked production from their tight ends earlier in the season, due in part to Chig Okonkwo’s injury. A system that was expected to include a heavy dose of multiple tight end sets has, according to TruMedia, used two or more tight ends on only 33.6 percent of its plays, a lower rate than last season (37 percent).
 “It’s a new offense still, from the perspective of big-picture types of things,” right guard Sam Cosmi said recently. “So, we’re still getting pieces here and there, just those little nuances.”

 Part of that is on Daniels, as he continues to develop in a system that Quinn believes will benefit him in the long run.
 “I would say there’s another level that he’s going to get to,” Quinn said, noting Daniels is still learning the balance of being decisive but not too antsy behind the line. “There are times where I’ve been like, ‘That’s it.’ There’s been other times where I’d say, ‘Be more decisive. Wait it out.’ … (But) he has definite call commands, knows what to do, what the play is. Like that part is clear.”
 Daniels’ transition is one many young quarterbacks face early in their NFL careers as they adapt to pro-style schemes, with under-center formations and built-in options to play calls. The job no longer requires the execution of one call; rather, it’s hearing the “if you see this, then do this, but if you see that, then do that” call, relaying it to 10 teammates and making sure each is clear on his specific role, then adapting on the fly if a defense presents a different picture post-snap — and doing all of this in mere seconds while 300-pound defensive linemen barrel toward them.
 Advertisement
 After the Commanders’ Week 7 loss in San Francisco, former quarterback turned broadcaster Kurt Warner criticized Daniels for playing it too safe instead of throwing in tighter windows and too often going for more conservative options instead of taking the bigger shot when it was there.
 Quinn agreed partly with Warner’s assessment, but noted some of the change needed to come from the entire operation, to help Daniels get in and out of the huddle quicker and to ensure his receivers are running the right routes at the right depths.

 How should the Commanders approach the trade deadline? Here are some options
 The Commanders have disappointed so far, but a weak division has kept their hopes afloat. So how should they approach the trade deadline?
 During the bye week, Quinn and his staff reviewed their systems and play calls to streamline and simplify the calls so that Daniels could get in and out of the huddle faster, leaving him more time to relay plays in the huddle and make adjustments at the line.
 “We’re able to get up there in those pressing seconds, of maybe you go from getting on the ball at 12 (seconds), and you get on the ball at 17,” Daniels said after the win over the Eagles on Sunday night. “Those five seconds make a big difference, just to communicate with the guys and give myself a chance to see what the defense is doing and have an idea of what they can do. So, that was huge for not only me, but just the offense, getting on the ball and playing with tempo (and) urgency.”
 Quinn has also lauded Daniels’ improvement in protecting himself and the ball. When he scrambles, he clearly is avoiding extra hits by sliding or getting down. And he’s the only qualified quarterback who hasn’t thrown an interception this season.
 But for the Commanders to continue to both evolve in Blough’s offense and keep their season alive, Quinn has stressed a need to play consistently and cleanly for a full game, something they’ve yet to do.
 Early in Sunday’s matchup with the Eagles, Daniels became so frustrated by penalties and self-inflicted setbacks that he lit into some of his teammates on the sideline, urging them to clean up their play.
 Advertisement
 “Honestly, it was complete BS, just how we started and what we were doing,” he said afterward. “… At that point, it wasn’t our brand of football that we want to play or showcase. It was at that point, you kind of just get frustrated, you go up and speak your mind. So, that’s kind of what I did. And kind of just help snap everybody back into place.”
 The moment showcased Daniels’ growth as a quarterback. But his future — and that of his young coordinator — will be dependent on building this Commanders’ offense into their own.
